clinicalPearls: The classic acid-base picture is a mixed primary respiratory alkalosis and primary high anion-gap metabolic acidosis, most evident in adults
Early features include tinnitus, deafness, nausea, vomiting, hyperventilation and hyperpyrexia
A normal or rising blood pH with low carbon dioxide reflects the respiratory alkalosis, but falling pH signals dangerous progression
A single salicylate concentration can mislead, so serial levels are needed because of delayed and erratic absorption, especially with enteric-coated preparations or bezoars
Concentrated liquid methyl salicylate (oil of wintergreen) can cause rapid severe toxicity from a small volume
Acidaemia increases the non-ionised fraction that crosses into the central nervous system, so intubation with inadequate ventilation can be catastrophic
Urinary alkalinisation enhances salicylate elimination and limits central penetration, while haemodialysis is used for severe toxicity, high levels or end-organ effects
Maintaining potassium is essential, as hypokalaemia prevents effective urinary alkalinisation
reference.pathophysiology: Salicylate directly stimulates the medullary respiratory centre, producing hyperventilation and a primary respiratory alkalosis. Simultaneously it uncouples oxidative phosphorylation, impairs the citric acid cycle and promotes accumulation of organic acids and lactate, generating a high anion-gap metabolic acidosis and heat production with hyperthermia. As pH falls, a greater proportion of salicylate becomes non-ionised and crosses the blood-brain barrier, worsening neurotoxicity. Salicylate also interferes with glucose metabolism, coagulation and gastrointestinal integrity, and in severe cases causes pulmonary and cerebral oedema.
additionalDifferentials: Diabetic or other high anion-gap ketoacidosis
Toxic alcohol (methanol or ethylene glycol) poisoning
Primary central nervous system infection causing hyperpnoea and confusion
additionalInvestigations: Serial serum salicylate concentrations to track absorption and elimination
Arterial blood gas with anion-gap and acid-base interpretation
Serum electrolytes, particularly potassium, and glucose
Coagulation profile and paracetamol level in intentional overdose
Chest radiograph if pulmonary oedema is suspected and urine pH monitoring during alkalinisation
redFlags: Altered mental status, seizures or coma indicating central nervous system toxicity
A falling or normalising pH after initial alkalosis, signalling decompensation
Hyperthermia, haemodynamic instability or intractable acidosis
Very high or rising salicylate concentrations, or need for airway control
reference.prognosis: Prompt recognition, urinary alkalinisation and timely haemodialysis when indicated usually yield good outcomes, but delayed treatment, marked acidaemia and central nervous system involvement are associated with high mortality.
pitfalls: Relying on a single salicylate level and missing continued absorption
Intubating and under-ventilating, causing acidaemia and rapid neurological deterioration
Allowing hypokalaemia, which defeats urinary alkalinisation
Misinterpreting the early respiratory alkalosis as reassuring
Delaying haemodialysis in patients with high levels or end-organ toxicity
management: Gastrointestinal decontamination with activated charcoal for recent significant ingestion, with consideration of repeated doses for enteric-coated preparations or a suspected bezoar
Urinary alkalinisation with intravenous sodium bicarbonate to enhance renal elimination of salicylate and reduce central nervous system penetration
Correction of hypokalaemia, which is essential for effective alkalinisation, alongside fluid resuscitation for volume depletion
Glucose supplementation to counter neuroglycopenia even when peripheral glucose appears adequate
Haemodialysis for severe toxicity, central nervous system features, pulmonary oedema, renal failure or refractory acidaemia
Avoidance of intubation where possible, and if unavoidable, maintenance of aggressive ventilation to prevent worsening acidaemia and neurotoxicity
Serial salicylate concentrations and arterial blood gas monitoring to track absorption, elimination and acid-base status
Early involvement of clinical toxicology and critical care for severe or progressive poisoning
